title_en: Ou Lizhen v. Gao Yan — dispute over liability for damage caused by domesticated animals
ruling_gist_en: In a dispute over liability for damage caused by domestic animals, if the domestic animal does not directly contact the victim, but causes the victim to fall and get injured due to dangerous actions such as chasing, approaching, etc., it shall be determined that there is a causal relationship between the dangerous actions and the occurrence of the damage. If the animal owner or manager fails to provide evidence to prove that the victim had intentional fault or gross negligence in causing the damage, they shall bear all the tort liability.
keywords_en: Civil; dispute over liability for damage caused by domestic animals; first instance; basic people's court; Guangdong Province; natural person; Tort Liability Law; determination of causation; definition of dangerous animal behavior; proof of victim's fault; in favor of plaintiff; dog chasing causing person to fall; no direct contact; failure to leash dog in public place; tort liability; Gao Yan's animal damage liability dispute
full_text_en:
Ou Lizhen v. Gao Yan — dispute over liability for damage caused by a domesticated animal

[Ruling Summary]

In cases involving disputes over liability for damage caused by domesticated animals, where the domesticated animal does not directly contact the victim, but the victim falls and is injured due to dangerous actions of the animal such as chasing or approaching, it shall be determined that a causal relationship exists between the animal and the physical harm suffered by the victim. If the animal's keeper or manager cannot prove that the victim intentionally or with gross negligence caused the damage, the keeper or manager shall bear full tort liability.

Plaintiff: Ou Lizhen, female, 62 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Yunfu City, Guangdong Province.

Defendant: Gao Yan, female, 27 years old, Tujia ethnicity, residing in Taishan City, Guangdong Province.

Plaintiff Ou Lizhen filed a lawsuit with the Taishan City People's Court, Guangdong Province, against Defendant Gao Yan regarding a dispute over liability for damage caused by a domesticated animal.

Plaintiff Ou Lizhen alleged: At approximately 8:00 p.m. on August 13, 2017, when Ou Lizhen was passing by the storefront of the Taicheng Xucheng Driving Training Information Consulting Service Center operated by Defendant Gao Yan, she was suddenly attacked by a dog kept by Gao Yan. Unable to evade, Ou Lizhen fell to the ground. That same evening, Ou Lizhen was immediately taken to the Taicheng District People's Hospital for hospitalization. A B-ultrasound examination diagnosed a fracture of the left intertrochanteric femur with separation of the fractured ends involving the greater trochanter, requiring immediate surgery. After the incident, Ou Lizhen's family called the police. The police station intervened and conducted an investigation. In the interview record, Gao Yan confirmed that she was the dog's owner and that the dog was not leashed at the time of the incident, and that Ou Lizhen's injury was caused by her dog. At the same time, Gao Yan provided the police station with surveillance footage from the time, which clearly showed Gao Yan's dog attacking Ou Lizhen. Due to Gao Yan's negligent supervision of her dog, causing Ou Lizhen to be injured by the dog, it not only caused Ou Lizhen physical pain and loss from missed work, but also caused Ou Lizhen great mental distress. The losses suffered by Ou Lizhen as a result include: medical expenses of RMB 56,000, follow-up treatment costs of RMB 15,000, disability compensation of RMB 135,663, disability appraisal fees of RMB 5,000, mental distress damages of RMB 30,000, hospitalization food subsidies of RMB 1,300, nutrition expenses of RMB 5,000, and transportation expenses of RMB 3,000, totaling RMB 250,963. The claims were: 1. Gao Yan shall compensate Ou Lizhen for hospitalization and medical expenses and other costs incurred due to the injury caused by Gao Yan's dog, totaling RMB 56,928.41 (including hospitalization medical expenses of RMB 50,328.41, hospitalization food subsidies of RMB 1,300, hospitalization nursing fees of RMB 1,300, transportation expenses of RMB 1,000, and nutrition expenses of RMB 3,000); 2. The litigation costs of this case shall be borne by Gao Yan. During the proceedings, on November 7, 2017, Ou Lizhen increased the claim in item 1 above to RMB 250,963.

Defendant Gao Yan defended: 1. In this case, Plaintiff Ou Lizhen's fall was unrelated to the pet dog. Since the pet dog never came into contact with Ou Lizhen, the key to determining whether there is a causal relationship between the damage and the pet dog lies in whether the pet dog posed a real danger to Ou Lizhen at the time of the incident, sufficient to cause Ou Lizhen to panic, thereby causing her to fall while evading. However, in this case, the pet dog did not chase, trip, or bark at Ou Lizhen, and there is no causal relationship with the harmful consequences. Specifically: (1) The pet dog's movement did not produce any startling effect. At the time of the incident, the pet dog moved forward a distance equal to its own body length, and it walked normally rather than charging or lunging forward. (2) The pet dog was far away from Ou Lizhen. Even if the pet dog took two steps forward, it still maintained a considerable distance from Ou Lizhen, much greater than the distance when Ou Lizhen first stopped in front of the chicken pot restaurant and passed by the dog. (3) Ou Lizhen was not, as she claimed, a person extremely afraid of dogs. At the beginning of the video, Ou Lizhen passed by and stopped outside the chicken pot restaurant, at which time she was relatively close to the pet dog. Later, Ou Lizhen looked directly at the pet dog and passed in front of it, showing interest in the dog rather than fear. The incident location was a wide sidewalk. A person afraid of dogs would, if given a choice, surely walk around the dog rather than take actions like Ou Lizhen approaching the dog and passing by. Considering the above three points together with the objective environment of the case, and comparing the actions of Ou Lizhen's husband, who was walking with her, at the time the pet dog moved, it is the normal reaction of an ordinary person in the on-site environment. The pet dog's movement could not possibly have startled a distant pedestrian and caused them to fall and be injured, and there is no causal relationship with the damage in this case. 2. The amount of compensation claimed by Ou Lizhen has no objective basis. Gao Yan does not recognize her claim for compensation and reiterates that the damage claimed by Ou Lizhen has no causal relationship with the pet dog. In view of the specific demands for compensation raised by Ou Lizhen, Gao Yan responds as follows: (1) Gao Yan does not recognize the relevant basis for the compensation claimed by Ou Lizhen and has submitted a written application for judicial appraisal to the court. (2) According to the compensation list provided by Ou Lizhen when she amended her claim, the medical expenses do not match the amounts on the receipts she provided; the follow-up medical expenses do not match the statements in the appraisal opinion she submitted; the disability compensation was based on an appraisal commissioned by Ou Lizhen herself; the disability appraisal fee does not match the invoice amount attached to the appraisal opinion submitted by Ou Lizhen; regarding mental distress damages, referring to Articles 9 and 10 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Determination of Compensation for Mental Distress in Civil Tort Liabilities*, disability compensation is comprehensive compensation that includes mental distress, so this item constitutes a duplicate claim, and Gao Yan also lacks the financial capacity to bear it; the hospitalization food subsidy was not caused by the pet dog; the nutrition expenses were not determined based on the opinion of a medical institution, which does not comply with Article 24 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Compensation for Personal Injury*; the transportation expenses lack formal receipts, and Ou Lizhen had no necessary reason to go to Foshan City for treatment, which does not comply with Article 22 of the said Interpretation.

[Facts Found at First Instance by the Taishan City People's Court]

The surveillance video provided by Defendant Gao Yan, which was not disputed by either party, clearly shows: At 19:20:20 on August 13, 2017, Plaintiff Ou Lizhen, accompanied by her husband, was walking on foot along the wide public sidewalk in front of No. 2 Shunde Road, Taicheng, Taishan City, at the juncture between the Xucheng Driving Training Information Consulting Service Center and the Juxianlou Restaurant. There, they encountered a brown "Teddy dog" kept by Gao Yan, which was resting on the steps. When the "Teddy dog" saw Ou Lizhen and her husband approaching, it stood up and took two steps (approximately 50 cm) in the direction of Ou Lizhen. At that time, the distance between Ou Lizhen and the "Teddy dog" was approximately 3 meters. When Ou Lizhen saw the "Teddy dog" approaching, she panicked and stepped to her left to avoid it, falling and injuring herself. After being injured, Ou Lizhen was immediately sent to Taishan People's Hospital for hospitalization. The next day, she was transferred to Foshan Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine for further hospitalization. She was hospitalized for a total of 13 days. The hospitalization medical expenses incurred were RMB 50,328.41. During the treatment period, there was no medical advice recommending enhanced nutritional support treatment. Guangdong Fawei Judicial Appraisal Institute accepted Ou Lizhen's commission on November 15, 2017, and issued a *Judicial Appraisal Opinion* on November 16 of the same month, appraising Ou Lizhen's injuries as: Level 9 disability; follow-up treatment costs approximately RMB 12,000. The appraisal fee incurred was RMB 3,000.

[Opinion of the Court at First Instance by the Taishan City People's Court]

A citizen's right of person is protected by law. If a domesticated animal causes harm to another person, the animal's keeper or manager shall bear tort liability. Based on Plaintiff Ou Lizhen's claims, as verified by the Taishan City People's Court, the losses, reduced income, and necessary increased expenses resulting from the accident are as follows: 1. Medical expenses: RMB 50,812.03 (including RMB 483.62 for outpatient fees and RMB 50,328.41 for hospitalization fees); 2. Follow-up treatment costs: RMB 12,000; 3. Disability compensation: RMB 135,663 (urban per capita disposable income for general areas of Guangdong Province in 2016: RMB 37,684.30/year × 18 years × 20% disability compensation coefficient); 4. Appraisal fee: RMB 3,000; 5. Mental distress damages: Pursuant to Article 10 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Determination of Compensation for Mental Distress in Civil Tort Liabilities*, the accident resulted in Ou Lizhen's disability, causing her significant mental suffering. Considering her disability level in the accident and the local living standards, mental distress damages are determined in the court's discretion at RMB 6,000; 6. Hospitalization food subsidy: RMB 1,300 (RMB 100/day × 13 days); 7. Transportation expenses: In the absence of relevant receipts provided by Ou Lizhen, the court of first instance, considering the number of follow-up visits and the length of hospitalization, determines this in its discretion at RMB 1,000. Total: RMB 209,775.03. According to Article 78 of the *Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China*, which provides: "If a domesticated animal causes harm to another person, the animal's keeper or manager shall bear tort liability, but if the damage is caused by the victim's intentional conduct or gross negligence, liability may be disclaimed or mitigated." The surveillance video provided by Defendant Gao Yan clearly shows that the dog kept by Gao Yan was a small, docile brown "Teddy dog." In this case, Gao Yan failed to take safety precautions, allowing the "Teddy dog" to roam freely in a public place and, when it approached Ou Lizhen, caused Ou Lizhen to fall and be injured due to fright. As the animal's keeper and manager, Gao Yan should bear corresponding liability. At the same time, under the circumstances where the "Teddy dog," upon seeing Ou Lizhen approaching, neither barked nor attacked Ou Lizhen, and only moved approximately 50 cm towards her while still maintaining a distance of about 3 meters from her, Ou Lizhen, due to excessive panic, took improper evasive action, fell, and injured herself. She herself was grossly negligent. Considering Ou Lizhen's gross negligence and the actual circumstances of this case, the court of first instance, in its discretion, finds it appropriate for Gao Yan to bear 30% liability for Ou Lizhen's losses of RMB 209,775.03, i.e., RMB 62,932.50 (RMB 209,775.03 × 30%). As for Ou Lizhen's other claims, they lack factual and legal basis, and the court does not support them.

In summary, the Taishan City People's Court, in accordance with Articles 16 and 78 of the *Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China*, Articles 17, 19, 22, 23, and 24 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Compensation for Personal Injury*, Article 8, Paragraph 2, and Article 10, Paragraph 1, of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Determination of Compensation for Mental Distress in Civil Tort Liabilities*, Article 64, Paragraph 1, of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, and Article 90 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, rendered the following judgment on July 10, 2018:

1. Defendant Gao Yan shall, within ten days from the date this judgment takes legal effect, compensate Plaintiff Ou Lizhen the amount of RMB 62,932.50;
2. Ou Lizhen's other claims are dismissed.

Both Ou Lizhen and Gao Yan were dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance and appealed to the Jiangmen Intermediate People's Court, Guangdong Province.

Ou Lizhen appealed, arguing: 1. Due to Gao Yan's negligent supervision of her dog, Ou Lizhen was injured by the dog, causing Ou Lizhen not only physical pain and loss from missed work, but also great mental distress. 2. Gao Yan failed to fulfill her basic responsibilities in managing the domesticated animal and should bear full liability for the accident, not secondary liability. However, the judgment of first instance, without any basis, determined that Ou Lizhen should bear 70% liability, which violates the principle of fairness and has no factual basis. Therefore, the judgment of first instance erred in fact-finding. 3. The application of law in the judgment of first instance was improper; this case involves special tort, and the court of first instance applied the law incorrectly. In summary, Ou Lizhen requested: 1. The original judgment be reversed; 2. The judgment be amended to order Gao Yan to pay RMB 250,963; 3. The litigation costs for the first and second instances be borne by Gao Yan.

Gao Yan responded, arguing: 1. There is no causal relationship between Ou Lizhen's fall and the dog. There is no evidence in this case proving that Ou Lizhen's fall was caused by the pet dog. 2. From the video, the change in Ou Lizhen's walking route shows that when passing by, she not only did not choose to avoid the pet dog but also intentionally chose a route close to the dog, indicating that Ou Lizhen is not, as she claimed, a person extremely afraid of dogs. 3. In the video, Ou Lizhen began to fall outside the frame and only came into the frame as she was about to hit the ground. It is impossible to know the cause of her fall; she could have tripped over a stone or been attacked by another animal or insect. In the video, the pet dog had no behavior such as attacking, threatening, or contacting, so this video cannot prove a causal relationship between the pet dog and Ou Lizhen's fall. 4. The incompleteness of the video makes it impossible to determine the true cause of Ou Lizhen's fall.

Gao Yan appealed, arguing: 1. The dog kept by Gao Yan did not commit any tortious act and has no causal relationship with Ou Lizhen's injury. Gao Yan should not bear tort liability as a matter of law. 2. Ou Lizhen's claim that she fell because she could not evade in time does not match the circumstances. 3. Relying on the *Judicial Appraisal Opinion* submitted solely by Ou Lizhen as the basis for compensation lacks objectivity. 4. In this case, mental distress has already been reflected in the form of disability compensation. The first instance judgment's determination of mental distress damages constitutes double counting. In summary, Gao Yan requested: 1. The first item of the original judgment be reversed and amended to dismiss all of Ou Lizhen's claims; 2. Ou Lizhen bear all litigation costs in this case.

Ou Lizhen responded, arguing: 1. This case involves special tort. Gao Yan confirmed that the pet dog was not leashed and was not restrained in any way, violating the relevant national laws and regulations on keeping domesticated animals. 2. Regarding the special case of animal tort in civil law, the burden of proof is reversed. Unless Gao Yan can prove the fault of the injured party or the fault of a third party or gross negligence. 3. Regarding Gao Yan's argument about Ou Lizhen's coming and going: because the store in question is in a pedestrian street, a public place, not Gao Yan's private premises, it was normal for Ou Lizhen to be farther from the store when going and closer to the store when returning walking on the right side. This does not indicate, as Gao Yan argues, that Ou Lizhen was not afraid of dogs.

[Facts Found at Second Instance by the Jiangmen Intermediate People's Court, Guangdong Province]

The court of second instance confirmed the facts found by the court of first instance.

Additionally found: During the period from 19:19:10 to 19:19:25, Ou Lizhen first appeared at the upper left of the screen. To avoid a vehicle coming from behind, she slowly walked in the direction of the lower right corner of the screen.

[Opinion of the Court of Second Instance by the Jiangmen Intermediate People's Court, Guangdong Province]

The issues in dispute between the parties in this case are: 1. Whether Appellant Gao Yan should bear tort liability for the losses of Appellant Ou Lizhen arising from this case; 2. If so, how should the amount of Ou Lizhen's losses be determined.

1. Whether Appellant Gao Yan should bear tort liability for the losses of Appellant Ou Lizhen arising from this case.

According to Article 78 of the *Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China*, which provides: "If a domesticated animal causes harm to another person, the animal's keeper or manager shall bear tort liability, but if there is evidence proving that the damage was caused by the victim's intentional conduct or gross negligence, liability may be disclaimed or mitigated," and Article 79, which provides: "If an animal causes harm to another person due to failure to take safety measures in violation of management regulations, the animal's keeper or manager shall bear tort liability," the animal's keeper or manager has the obligation to keep or manage the animal in accordance with regulations and to take safety measures for the animal. If the animal they keep or manage causes harm to another person, the animal's keeper or manager shall bear tort liability. Liability may be mitigated only if the victim acted intentionally or with gross negligence. In this case, at 19:20:20 on August 13, 2017, Appellant Ou Lizhen, accompanied by her husband, was walking on foot along the wide public sidewalk in front of No. 2 Shunde Road, Taicheng, Taishan City, at the juncture between the Xucheng Driving Training Information Consulting Service Center and the Juxianlou Restaurant. There, they encountered a "Teddy dog" kept by Appellant Gao Yan, which was resting on the steps. When the "Teddy dog" saw Ou Lizhen and her husband approaching, it stood up and took two steps in the direction of Ou Lizhen. When Ou Lizhen saw the "Teddy dog" approaching, she stepped to her left to avoid it, fell, and was injured, resulting in the losses at issue in this case. Gao Yan appealed, arguing that her "Teddy dog" did not engage in actions such as "chasing, pouncing, biting, or barking," and that Ou Lizhen fell on her own, so she should not bear compensation liability. Ou Lizhen, on the other hand, argued that Gao Yan failed to leash her dog or take any restraint, and that the aggressive behavior of the dog caused Ou Lizhen to fall, leading to the losses. Regarding the issue in dispute between the parties, the court of second instance analyzes as follows: First, Gao Yan has no evidence that her "Teddy dog" obtained a *Dog Keeping Permit*. Her keeping of the dog violated Article 4 of the *Guangdong Province Dog Management Regulations*, which provides: "County-level cities and above (including county towns and suburbs), industrial and mining areas, ports, airports, scenic spots and areas within 3 kilometers thereof, economic development zones, and townships where various types of foreign economic cooperation exist are classified as dog-prohibited areas. Government agencies, foreign institutions in Guangdong, and foreign nationals in the above areas who need to keep dogs due to special circumstances must obtain approval from the local public security department, obtain a *Dog Keeping Permit*, and have the dog immunized before they may keep it confined or leashed." Second, although the dog in this case did not perform such actions as "scratching, pouncing, or biting" that directly contacted the person, when an unfamiliar dog, especially an unrestrained dog, enters a person's safety zone, it is instinctive for an ordinary person to feel fear. Therefore, when Ou Lizhen saw the unrestrained dog suddenly stand up and approach her, she instinctively feared, evaded, fell, and was injured. Although there was no actual physical contact between the dog and the person, a relationship of cause and effect existed between the injury and the dog, and the animal's keeper or manager should also bear tort liability for this. Third, Gao Yan argued that Ou Lizhen's fall might have been caused by tripping over a stone or by an attack from another animal, but she did not provide any evidence to support her claim. Furthermore, there is no evidence that Ou Lizhen intentionally or with gross negligence provoked, struck, chased, or engaged in similar conduct during the incident. Based on this, it can be determined that the losses incurred by Ou Lizhen in this case were caused by Gao Yan's failure to properly keep the animal. In this case, there is also no evidence showing circumstances that would mitigate Gao Yan's liability. Therefore, Gao Yan shall bear full compensation liability for Ou Lizhen's losses. The court of first instance determined that Ou Lizhen, due to excessive panic, fell and injured herself, constituting gross negligence, and attributed 70% liability to Ou Lizhen herself. This constituted an error in the application of law, which the court of second instance hereby corrects.

2. The determination of the amount of Appellant Ou Lizhen's losses.

During the second instance, both parties raised no objections to the following amounts determined by the first-instance court: medical expenses of RMB 50,328.41, hospital meal subsidies of RMB 1,300, transportation expenses of RMB 1,000, follow-up treatment expenses of RMB 12,000, and appraisal fees of RMB 3,000. The second-instance court confirmed these amounts. With respect to the disability compensation, Appellant Gao Yan challenged the conclusion of the Judicial Expertise Opinion (Yue Wei Si Jian Suo [2017] Lin Jian Zi No. 11423) issued by Guangdong Fawei Judicial Appraisal Institute, which determined that Ou Lizhen had a Class 9 disability, and requested a re-appraisal. Upon review, the Guangdong Fawei Judicial Appraisal Institute is an appraisal institution qualified to conduct appraisals, and its appraisers also possess the requisite qualifications. The Institute used the medical records of Appellant Ou Lizhen as the basis for the appraisal, applied professional knowledge and skills after conducting a physical examination, and, in accordance with Article 5.9.6.9 of the "Classification of the Degree of Disability Caused by Human Injury," produced the Judicial Expertise Opinion (Yue Wei Si Jian Suo [2017] Lin Jian Zi No. 11423) through legally prescribed procedures. The Opinion is compliant with relevant legal provisions in terms of form, process, basis, content, and conclusions, and is free from defects; it may be used as evidence in this case to establish the facts. Although Gao Yan appealed, challenging the conclusion of the Judicial Expertise Opinion and requesting a re-appraisal, she failed to provide rebuttal evidence proving that the Judicial Expertise Opinion suffered from serious procedural violations or insufficient factual basis, or that there were other circumstances rendering it inadmissible as evidence. Therefore, the grounds of her appeal are untenable and are not supported by the second-instance court. Accordingly, the first-instance court's calculation of Ou Lizhen's disability compensation as RMB 135,663 (RMB 37,684.30 per year × 18 years × 20% disability coefficient, based on the per capita disposable income of urban residents in general areas of Guangdong Province in 2016) was not erroneous, and the second-instance court confirms this amount. As for the mental distress damages, the first-instance court, in accordance with Article 22 of the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "where a tort infringes upon another's personal rights or interests and causes serious mental harm, the infringed person may claim mental distress damages," and considering the circumstances of Ou Lizhen's disability, determined the amount to be RMB 6,000, which was also not inappropriate. The second-instance court upholds this determination. Accordingly, the total amount of losses suffered by Ou Lizhen in this case is RMB 209,775.03 (RMB 50,812.03 + RMB 6,000 + RMB 1,300 + RMB 1,000 + RMB 12,000 + RMB 3,000 + RMB 135,663). Ou Lizhen's claims exceeding this amount lack factual and legal basis and are not supported by the second-instance court.

In summary, part of Appellant Ou Lizhen's appeal is well-founded and should be upheld; Appellant Gao Yan's appeal lacks sufficient grounds and is not upheld. The Jiangmen Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province, in accordance with Article 22, Article 78, and Article 79 of the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item 2 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 90 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on December 13, 2018:

1. The civil judgment (2017) Yue 0781 Min Chu No. 2581 of the Taishan People's Court of Guangdong Province is set aside;

2. Gao Yan shall pay RMB 209,775.03 to Ou Lizhen within ten days from the date this judgment takes effect;

3. All other claims of Ou Lizhen are dismissed.

This judgment is final.
